title: Databases
tagline: The relational model, SQL, conceptual design, normalisation, storage and indexing, query processing and optimisation, transactions and recovery
summary: Databases store the data that organisations depend on and answer questions about it efficiently and reliably. This course covers the relational model and relational algebra, SQL, conceptual design and normalisation, and then how a database engine works inside: storage and indexing, query processing and optimisation, transactions and concurrency control, and crash recovery.
overview: A **database system** stores the data an organisation depends on — students and grades, accounts and payments, orders and stock — and answers questions about it quickly and correctly while many programs read and change it at once and machines fail. The relational approach, which has dominated since the 1980s, separates *what* the data means from *how* it is stored: data is modelled as tables, queries are written in a declarative language, SQL, and the system decides how to evaluate them. This course teaches both sides: how to model, constrain and query data, and how a database engine works inside to make those queries fast and those updates safe.

The first half is about the logical level. [[databases/relational-model]] defines relations, keys and the relational algebra, and proves what the algebra can and cannot express; [[databases/sql]] teaches SQL with its bag semantics, three-valued logic for nulls, aggregation, subqueries and recursive queries, with every query run in SQLite; [[databases/conceptual-design]] turns requirements into entity–relationship designs and tables; and [[databases/normalisation]] uses functional dependencies, Armstrong's axioms and the BCNF and 3NF decomposition algorithms, with proofs of losslessness and dependency preservation. The second half opens the engine: pages, buffer management and B+-tree and hash indexes ([[databases/storage-indexing]]), algorithms for sorting and joins with their I/O costs ([[databases/query-processing]]), cost-based optimisation with cardinality estimates and System R's dynamic programming ([[databases/query-optimisation]]), serialisability, two-phase locking, isolation levels and snapshot isolation ([[databases/transactions]]), and write-ahead logging and the ARIES recovery algorithm ([[databases/recovery]]).

What makes the subject hard is that small differences in meaning have large consequences: a `NOT IN` over a column with a null, a lossy decomposition, an unclustered index used for a large range, an isolation level that permits write skew. The way through is to be precise — state what a query, a constraint or a schedule means, then check it on a small instance by hand and by running it. Do the cost calculations with real numbers, trace the algorithms (closure, BCNF decomposition, external sorting, ARIES) step by step, and run the SQL and Python listings. The prerequisite is [[data-structures]], in particular balanced search trees and hash tables, together with the sets, relations and logic of [Maths Atlas](/learn/maths/).
outcomes: Define relations, keys and foreign keys, write queries in relational algebra, and prove algebraic equivalences and limits of expressiveness such as the monotonicity of difference-free queries.
Write correct SQL queries with joins, outer joins, aggregation, nested and recursive queries, and explain their results under bag semantics and three-valued logic, including the pitfalls of nulls.
Design an entity–relationship model from requirements, choosing cardinality and participation constraints, and translate it into relational schemas with keys and referential constraints.
Compute attribute closures, candidate keys and minimal covers, test normal forms, and decompose schemas into BCNF or 3NF with proofs of lossless join and dependency preservation.
Explain record and page layouts and buffer replacement, and calculate the height, size and I/O cost of B+-tree and hash indexes, including when an index is worse than a scan.
Analyse the I/O cost of external sorting and of nested-loop, index, sort-merge and hash joins, and choose an algorithm for given sizes and memory.
Apply equivalence rules and cardinality estimation to compare query plans, and carry out System R-style dynamic programming for join ordering.
Test schedules for conflict serialisability with precedence graphs, prove that two-phase locking guarantees it, and handle deadlocks and phantoms.
Distinguish the SQL isolation levels from the guarantees of real systems, and explain snapshot isolation, its write-skew anomaly and serializable snapshot isolation.
Explain write-ahead logging and checkpoints, and trace the analysis, redo and undo passes of ARIES, including compensation log records and repeated crashes.

chapters.title: The relational model
chapters.summary: Relations, keys and integrity constraints, and the relational algebra.

chapters.title: SQL
chapters.summary: Queries and joins, aggregation and grouping, nested queries, NULL values and views.

chapters.title: Conceptual design
chapters.summary: Entity–relationship modelling and translating a design into relational schemas.

chapters.title: Functional dependencies and normalisation
chapters.summary: Functional dependencies and anomalies, Boyce–Codd and third normal forms, and lossless decompositions.

chapters.title: Storage and indexing
chapters.summary: Pages and records, buffer management, and B+-tree and hash indexes.

chapters.title: Query processing
chapters.summary: Algorithms for selection, sorting and joins, and their costs.

chapters.title: Query optimisation
chapters.summary: Equivalence rules, cardinality estimation and cost-based choice of query plans.

chapters.title: Transactions and concurrency control
chapters.summary: ACID properties, serialisability, two-phase locking, isolation levels and multiversion concurrency control.

chapters.title: Crash recovery
chapters.summary: Logging, write-ahead logging and checkpoints, and the ARIES recovery algorithm.

history.title: The relational model
history.detail: Edgar F. Codd's 'A relational model of data for large shared data banks' in Communications of the ACM proposed storing data as relations and querying it independently of its physical layout.

history.title: B-trees
history.detail: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight published 'Organization and maintenance of large ordered indexes' in Acta Informatica, introducing the balanced multiway trees that, as B+-trees, became the standard database index.

history.title: SEQUEL
history.detail: Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce described SEQUEL, the structured English query language for IBM's System R that became SQL.

history.title: Serialisability and two-phase locking
history.detail: Kapali Eswaran, Jim Gray, Raymond Lorie and Irving Traiger's 'The notions of consistency and predicate locks in a database system' defined serialisability, proved that two-phase locking ensures it, and identified phantoms.

history.title: The entity–relationship model
history.detail: Peter Chen's 'The entity-relationship model — toward a unified view of data' in ACM Transactions on Database Systems introduced ER modelling and its diagrams.

history.title: Cost-based query optimisation
history.detail: Patricia Selinger and colleagues' 'Access path selection in a relational database management system' described System R's optimiser: statistics, selectivity estimates and dynamic programming over join orders.

history.title: The SQL standard
history.detail: ANSI published the first SQL standard (adopted by ISO in 1987); later revisions added explicit joins (SQL-92), recursive queries (SQL:1999) and window functions (SQL:2003).

history.title: ARIES
history.detail: C. Mohan, Don Haderle, Bruce Lindsay, Hamid Pirahesh and Peter Schwarz published the ARIES recovery method in ACM Transactions on Database Systems: write-ahead logging, repeating history and compensation log records.

history.title: A critique of the SQL isolation levels
history.detail: Hal Berenson, Phil Bernstein, Jim Gray, Jim Melton, Elizabeth O'Neil and Patrick O'Neil showed that the ANSI isolation levels were ambiguous, and defined snapshot isolation and its write-skew anomaly.

history.title: Serializable snapshot isolation
history.detail: Michael Cahill, Uwe Röhm and Alan Fekete showed how to make snapshot isolation serialisable by detecting dangerous read–write dependencies at run time; PostgreSQL adopted the method in version 9.1 (2011).

references.title: Database System Concepts
references.authors: Abraham Silberschatz, Henry F. Korth, S. Sudarshan
references.note: Seventh edition. The most widely used comprehensive textbook: relational model, SQL, ER design and normalisation, storage, indexing, query processing and optimisation, transactions and recovery, with a running university example.

references.title: Database Management Systems
references.note: Third edition. Especially strong on the engine: the I/O cost model, external sorting, join algorithms, B+-trees and extendible hashing, and a clear chapter on ARIES.

references.title: Database Systems: The Complete Book
references.authors: Hector Garcia-Molina, Jeffrey D. Ullman, Jennifer Widom
references.note: Second edition. Rigorous on design theory (functional and multivalued dependencies, the chase), relational algebra and query compilation, and on logging, concurrency control and recovery.

references.title: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques
references.note: The classic treatise on transactions: locking, logging, recovery and the engineering of transaction-processing systems, by two of their architects.

references.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
references.note: How databases are used and built in modern systems: storage engines (B-trees and LSM trees), replication, partitioning, isolation levels and anomalies such as write skew, and distributed consistency.

references.title: Foundations of Databases
references.authors: Serge Abiteboul, Richard Hull, Victor Vianu
references.note: The theory of the relational model: algebra and calculus, expressive power, recursion and Datalog, and dependency theory; for readers who want full proofs.
